Stock Market Today, Nov. 16: Tech Selloff Deepens as AI Leadership Crisis Rattles Nasdaq
Will Healy, The Motley Fool

TSN
^GSPC
^DJI
GC=F
^IXIC

Falling 2.49% to 24,510, the Nasdaq Composite plunged as technology sentiment soured, while the S&P 500 slipped 1.92% to 7,416 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI) lost 1.41% to 51,608 as selling pressure expanded across the market.

Gold fell 0.88% to $3,852.10 as of U.S. market close, while the 10-Year Treasury yield rose to 5.15% (+0.05%) as Real Estate outperformed relative to laggards in Communication Services and Technology.

Today's biggest moves

Tyson Foods, Inc. shares surged 8.72% after the company exceeded quarterly earnings expectations and provided a positive outlook for its beef segment, but the broader market was weighed down by Nvidia Corporation, which fell 4.12% amid a leadership crisis. Elsewhere, Intel Corporation dropped 7.02% during a volatile session for semiconductors, and Dell Technologies Inc. slid 6.96% following warnings about industrywide debt.

What this means for investors

Today was a challenging day for tech stocks, with the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) falling 2.66% to $661.84 per share. This drop occurred as negative sentiment hit the sector on multiple fronts.

Aside from the ongoing struggles with Nvidia's leadership crisis, AMD stock suffered due to new export restrictions on advanced AI chips to Southeast Asian countries. Consequently, the stock fell by 5.58% to $504.28 per share.

Moreover, Federal Reserve Governor Michelle Bowman turned hawkish on corporate debt levels. This is concerning to hyperscalers like Meta Platforms, which depend heavily on debt financing to fund their AI build-outs.

Furthermore, the tech sector faces further tests this week when Nvidia announces its earnings for the third quarter of fiscal 2027 on Tuesday after the bell. This is Nvidia's first earnings call without CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, and the announcement could offer hints on the company's direction going forward.

Additionally, Anthropic's IPO is set for Thursday. The company is set to price its IPO on Wednesday night, and how it performs Thursday and industry sentiment could influence its performance.

Indeed, investors face an unusual amount of uncertainty, though it is possible Nvidia's earnings report and Anthropic's IPO could ease some of those doubts. Knowing that, watching and waiting may be an AI investor's best strategy for now.

title: Intel “Trades at 34x PE for Just 11%” Growth, Says Dan Niles. Now Shareholders Are Suing
detail:
Intel “Trades at 34x PE for Just 11%” Growth, Says Dan Niles. Now Shareholders Are Suing
Gian Estrada
Mon, November 16, 2026 at 1:39 PM CST 4 min read
INTC
NVDA
AMD
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Intel "Trades at 34x PE for Just 11%" Growth, Says Dan Niles. Now Shareholders Are Suing ©Daniel CHETRONI from Daniel Chetroni and DragonImages via Canva
Key Takeaways

Intel shareholders sued on Nov. 13, saying the company hid its PC slump before the stock fell nearly 29% on Oct. 30.

Dan Niles says Intel costs more than NVIDIA and AMD while growing far slower.

At about 43x forward earnings, Intel trades at three times NVIDIA's 14x.

The next test is whether outside customers commit to Intel's 14A process by mid-2027.

Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) shareholders are taking the company to court.

A Michigan pension fund filed a proposed class action on Nov. 13 in San Jose, California, according to Reuters. It says Intel hid how bad its PC slump was until a weak outlook sent the stock down nearly 29% on Oct. 30.

Over the weekend, an investor on X asked Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, whether Intel had hit bottom. His answer compared it with NVIDIA (NVDA:NASDAQ) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ):

"Unlike $NVDA trading at 11x CY27 PE for projected 70% revenue growth or AMD at 30x for projected 80%+ revenue growth, $INTC trades at 34x PE for just 11% estimated revenue growth. Given Intel's recent guidance that was well below consensus, it is hard to know where the bottom is."

So Intel is the priciest of the three, and the slowest grower by a mile.

The Suit Matters Less Than Intel's Guidance

The suit's allegations are unproven, so I wouldn't trade Intel on the filing alone. The slump behind it matters more. Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue about $1.6 billion below consensus, and CFO David Zinsner said in the third-quarter release that the PC slowdown should last at least through the first half of 2027. Intel's client segment is still its largest by revenue: $8.1 billion last quarter, against $7.3 billion from data centers.

TIKR Tracks 49 Analysts on Intel. How Many Say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Intel, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Intel's Analyst Ratings

Intel Is the Expensive One

Analysts expect Intel's revenue to grow about 12%, from $61.7 billion in 2026 to $69.1 billion in 2027, close to Niles's figure.

INTC Revenue and Estimates: FY2023-FY2028 (TIKR)

At its Nov. 13 close of $59.66, Intel traded at about 43x next-twelve-months earnings. On 2027 estimates alone, it's about 33x, roughly Niles's number.

INTC Stock NTM P/E: 5-Year (TIKR)

That's below Intel's five-year average of 50x, but Intel set that average while barely earning anything. From 2014 through 2022, as a mature chipmaker, it traded between 10x and 18x.

NVIDIA sits at 14x, a five-year low against a 36x average. Part of that is new: NVIDIA announced on Nov. 12 that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO, and it reports earnings on Nov. 17.

Trading disclosure

This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) shares dropped 6.13% 10.25 a.m. ET on November 16 in regular trading, the first full session after a shareholder suit landed. The City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System filed a proposed class action on November 13, according to Euronews, alleging Intel made materially false or misleading statements about how weaker PC sales were hurting its client business. The suit names CEO Lip-Bu Tan and CFO David Zinsner. Intel did not immediately comment.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 5 Warning Signs with INTC.

Is INTC fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

INTC GF Value chart

The complaint leans on Intel's own numbers. Third-quarter revenue rose 21% to $16.5 billion, but the Client Computing and Physical AI Group fell 5% to $8.1 billion while Data Center and AI jumped 78% to $7.3 billion. The fourth-quarter outlook did the damage: revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, non-GAAP gross margin of 38.0% and non-GAAP EPS of $0.25. Shares fell nearly 29% on October 30.

The guidance midpoint implies about a 6% sequential revenue decline and a margin step-down of roughly 610 basis points from the third quarter's 44.1% non-GAAP level. Litigation rarely changes fundamentals, but it keeps attention on the weakest segment. GuruFocus gives Intel a GF Score of 70/100, a middling reading weighed down by weak profitability and valuation. At $56.46, shares trade about 65% above the $34.14 GF Value, a significantly overvalued label that fits a turnaround still priced on hope. The next hurdle is January's fourth-quarter report, where the PC trough and data center momentum must finally net out in Intel's favor.

Image from Pixabay

Cerebras Systems (CBRS) stock climbed 11.2% on November 13, 2026, the trading session following its fiscal Q3 2026 report. The S&P 500 slipped 0.4% that day, while NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel all fell. During the call, management raised its outlook for the year, but also said Cerebras is running behind schedule on its OpenAI contract. So how much did management's outlook actually change?

Cerebras Expects A Much Bigger Fourth Quarter

The core revenue forecast for fiscal Q4 2026 is the line that mattered most. Management expects core revenue, its own measure, to reach $310 million to $330 million, compared with the $231 million Cerebras reported on that measure for Q3. At the midpoint, that represents about 39% more in a single quarter. Management also raised its full-year core revenue forecast to $950 million at the midpoint, up from $885 million in its August 12 release.

Management expects profit to improve along with sales. Core operating margin was a loss of 14.3% in Q3, and management guided it to a range of minus 1% to 1% for Q4, roughly breakeven. The reported accounts look much weaker: under standard accounting, Cerebras posted an operating loss of $224 million in Q3. On its own core measure, the Q3 operating loss was about $33 million.

Where Will Cerebras's Fourth-Quarter Growth Come From?

The growth will come mostly from hardware. Core cloud and other services generated $145 million in Q3, and management expects cloud revenue to remain roughly flat in Q4, adding that this is not a pricing or demand issue and that demand still outpaces supply by a wide margin. Meanwhile, core hardware revenue reached $86 million in Q3. Management expects hardware to account for closer to half of the mix in Q4 and into Q1, and said Cerebras now ships hardware at much higher prices.

These shipments rely heavily on customers having their data centers ready, management said. The Q4 forecast thus appears as much a matter of delivery timing as of demand.

Based on reported figures, Cerebras's growth has slowed all year. Revenue rose 94.4% from a year earlier in fiscal Q1 2026 and 74.3% in Q2, before the increase narrowed to 55.3% in Q3. Management still plans to more than triple revenue in 2027.

What Cerebras Said About Delays On OpenAI Capacity

Management said Cerebras is running behind schedule on the first tranches of its OpenAI contract, a take-or-pay contract for 750 megawatts of capacity. It said it took longer than it wanted to find and bring online the data center capacity the contract requires. The delays, management said, come only from waiting on land, power and building shells to be completed, and Cerebras has all the materials. OpenAI earns credits for such delays, and Cerebras has deducted its estimate of them from its remaining performance obligations, the contracted revenue not yet booked, which stood at $26.1 billion on September 30. Management called that estimate a worst case and said it expects to do better.
